upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-2-2.plain: The foam on that water hardened and became the earth. Death rested on the earth, and from his heat came Agni, the god of fire, full of light.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-2-3.plain: That fiery being split into three: fire, the sun and the air. Its body was spread across the directions, sky and earth, and whoever knows this stands firm wherever he goes.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-2-4.plain: Death wanted a second body, so in his mind he joined with Speech, and from this the year was born. When the newborn year came out, Death opened his mouth to swallow it, and the child cried 'Bhan!', which became speech.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-2-5.plain: Death thought that if he ate the child he would have little food, so instead he created everything—the sacred hymns, rituals, people and animals—and set out to eat it all. That is why he is called Aditi, from the word 'to eat,' and whoever knows this can enjoy everything.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-2-6.plain: Death wanted to perform an even bigger sacrifice, so he worked hard and practiced strict discipline. As he did, his strength, meaning his senses, left him, his body began to swell, and his mind stayed inside it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-13.plain: When the life-breath began to leave the body, it pulled all the senses loose, like a strong horse pulling up the pegs it is tied to. The senses begged it to stay, saying they could not live without it, and agreed to give it an offering.
themes: the senses argue over who matters most

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-14.plain: Each sense admits that its own gift really belongs to the breath: speech, sight, hearing, mind and the power to have children all depend on it. They say all food in the world is the breath's food and water is its clothing. This is why learned Vedic priests sip water before and after eating, to 'dress' the breath.
themes: giving credit where it is due

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-1.plain: Svetaketu, a young man, visits the land of the Panchalas and meets King Pravahana Jaivali. The king asks if his father has taught him, and Svetaketu says yes.
themes: a young man meets a king
being tested on what you know

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-2.plain: The king asks Svetaketu five deep questions: where people go after death, how they come back, why the other world never fills up, how water takes on a human voice, and what leads people to the path of the gods or the path of the ancestors. Svetaketu admits he cannot answer any of them.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-3.plain: Svetaketu refuses the king's hospitality and runs home upset. He complains to his father that he was called well-taught, yet could not answer a single one of the king's questions.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-4.plain: His father Gautama says he taught his son everything he knew, and suggests they both go to the king as students. The son refuses, so Gautama goes alone, and the king welcomes him with honor and offers him a gift.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-5.plain: Gautama asks for his gift to be the teaching the king spoke of to his son.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-6.plain: The king replies that this is a divine gift and asks Gautama to pick an ordinary human gift instead.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-7.plain: Gautama says he already has plenty of gold, cattle and possessions and wants no more. When the king asks if he truly seeks to learn, Gautama humbly comes to him as a student, and he really lived as one, not just in words.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-8.plain: The king asks Gautama not to be offended, explaining that this knowledge had never before belonged to any Brahmin priest. Still, he agrees to teach him because Gautama asked so sincerely.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-9.plain: The king begins his teaching by describing the sky as a sacred fire, with the sun as its fuel and the day as its light. The gods offer faith into this fire, and from it the moon arises.
themes: the universe as a sacred offering

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-10.plain: Next the rain god is pictured as a sacred fire, with clouds as smoke and lightning as light. The gods offer the moon into it, and rain is born.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-11.plain: This world is pictured as a sacred fire, with the earth as fuel and the stars as sparks. The gods offer rain into it, and food grows.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-12.plain: A man is pictured as a sacred fire, with his mouth, breath, tongue, eyes and ears as its parts. The gods offer food into him, and from that comes the seed of new life.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-13.plain: A woman is pictured as a sacred fire, and when seed is offered into her, a child is born. That person lives out their life, and then dies.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-14.plain: When a person dies, they are placed on the funeral fire, which is now a real fire. The gods offer the person into it, and from it the person rises shining and bright.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-15.plain: Those who understand this teaching, and those who worship faith and the True in the forest, travel after death along a path of light through day, the bright half of the moon, the sun and lightning. A spirit leads them to the worlds of Brahman, where they live for ages and never return.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-2-16.plain: Those who earn good results through rituals, charity and self-discipline travel by a darker path to the moon, where they stay until their good deeds run out. Then they come back as rain, become food, and are born again, going round the same cycle. Those who follow neither path are reborn as worms, birds and insects.
themes: the cycle of life and death

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-1.plain: Students of sacred knowledge ask big questions: Is Brahman, the ultimate reality, the cause of everything? Where do we come from, what keeps us alive, and where are we going? Who rules over our lives in both pain and joy?

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-2.plain: The students wonder if the cause of everything is time, nature, fate, chance, the elements, or a conscious person. None of these alone, or even together, seems to stand on its own, and the individual self also seems powerless over good and bad things.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-2-7.plain: Prajapati, the creator (here also seen as Death), wanted his swollen body to be fit for sacrifice, so it became a horse. That is how the great horse sacrifice, the Ashvamedha, got its name. The passage then says the sun is really this sacrifice and fire is the sacred fire, and both are one god, Death. Whoever understands this is no longer touched by death, because death has become his own Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-1.plain: The creator had two families of children: the Devas (gods) and the Asuras (demons). The Asuras were older. The Devas were fighting them and decided to win by singing the udgitha, a sacred chant sung during the sacrifice.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-2.plain: The gods asked Speech to sing the chant for them, and she did. But she also kept some of the joy of speaking well for herself. The demons saw their chance and struck her with evil. That is why speech can now say bad and hurtful things.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-3.plain: Next the gods asked the sense of smell to sing. It also kept some of the pleasure of smelling for itself. So the demons struck it with evil, and that is why we can smell bad things.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-4.plain: Then the gods asked the eye to sing. The eye kept some of the pleasure of seeing for itself. So the demons struck it with evil, and that is why we can see bad things.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-5.plain: Then the gods asked the ear to sing. The ear kept some of the pleasure of hearing for itself. So the demons struck it with evil, and that is why we can hear bad things.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-6.plain: Then the gods asked the mind to sing. The mind kept some of the pleasure of thinking for itself. So the demons struck it with evil, and that is why we can think bad thoughts. In this way the demons spoiled all these powers with evil.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-7.plain: Finally the gods asked the main breath, the life-breath in the mouth, to sing. When the demons attacked it, they shattered like a clump of earth thrown against a rock. So the gods won and the demons fell. Whoever knows this rises, and their enemies fall.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-8.plain: The gods asked who had stood by them so firmly. It was the breath inside the mouth, so it is called Ayasya. It is also the life-juice of the body's limbs, so it is called Angirasa.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-9.plain: This breath is also called Dur, meaning "far," because death stays far from it. Death stays far from anyone who knows this.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-10.plain: The breath took away the evil and death from the other powers and sent them to the far edges of the earth, and left their sins there. So people are told not to go to a man there, and not to go to those far ends, so they do not meet that evil and death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-11.plain: After taking away their evil and death, the breath carried the other powers beyond death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-12.plain: The breath carried Speech across death first. Free from death, speech became Agni, the god of fire, and now shines.
themes: how the senses relate to nature

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-13.plain: Next the breath carried the sense of smell across death. Free from death, it became Vayu, the wind, and now blows.
themes: how the senses relate to nature

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-14.plain: Next the breath carried the eye across death. Free from death, it became Aditya, the sun, and now burns bright.
themes: how the senses relate to nature

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-15.plain: Next the breath carried the ear across death. Free from death, it became the directions of space all around us.
themes: how the senses relate to nature

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-16.plain: Last, the breath carried the mind across death. Free from death, it became the moon, and now shines. In the same way, this breath carries anyone who knows this beyond death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-17.plain: By its singing, the breath also won food for itself, because all food is eaten through the breath. The other powers asked for a share, so the breath invited them to enter it. That is why, when the breath takes in food, all the senses are fed too.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-18.plain: A person who understands this becomes like the breath for their family: their support and leader. Anyone in the family who opposes such a person cannot even take care of their own people. But whoever follows and works with them can provide for those who depend on them.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-19.plain: The breath is called Ayasya Angirasa because it is the life-juice of the limbs. Whatever part of the body the breath leaves, that part dries up and withers.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-3.plain: Wise people who practiced deep meditation found the answer. They saw that God's own power is hidden inside the world's qualities, and that one God is in charge of all the other possible causes, like time and the self.
themes: is there a God behind everything
searching for the cause of life

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-4.plain: The sages describe God as a great wheel, made of many parts in groups of three, sixteen, fifty, twenty and eight. The wheel has one rope with many strands and moves along three roads. The picture shows that the whole complicated world turns on God.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-5.plain: Life is pictured as a wild, winding river. Its streams and springs are the five senses, its waves are the five breaths of life, and its source is the mind. Its rapids and whirlpools are the many kinds of pain and suffering people go through.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-6.plain: All beings live inside a huge turning wheel of life. The soul flutters about like a restless bird as long as it thinks it is separate from God, who turns the wheel. When God blesses it, the soul becomes free from death.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-7.plain: What the scriptures praise most is the Highest Brahman, the one ultimate reality. It holds a group of three within it. It never perishes and is a safe support. Students who come to know what is inside this world become devoted, merge into Brahman, and are not born again.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-8.plain: God holds everything together, both what changes and what never changes, both what is seen and what is unseen. The soul feels trapped because it must live with the results of its actions. When it comes to know God, it is freed from everything that binds it.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-9.plain: Three things have always existed. There is God, who knows everything and is strong. There is the soul, which does not yet know and is weak. And there is nature, through which each person gets the results of their deeds. Behind them all is the endless Self, present in every form but not acting itself. Whoever understands these three knows Brahman.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-10.plain: Matter, the stuff of the world, wears away. God, here called Hara, does not die. The one God rules both matter and the soul. By meditating on God and becoming one with him, all false appearances finally come to an end.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-11.plain: When a person truly knows God, all chains fall away, suffering ends, and birth and death stop. Meditating on God can bring a third state after death, power over everything. But only the one who stands alone is truly satisfied.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-12.plain: The reality that always rests inside you is the one thing worth knowing, and nothing beyond it needs to be known. Everything is made of three parts: the one who experiences, what is experienced, and the ruler over both. All three together are Brahman.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-13.plain: Fire is hidden in wood. You cannot see it, but it is there, and you bring it out by rubbing sticks together again and again. In the same way, the Self is hidden in the body and is brought out by repeating the sacred sound Om.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-14.plain: Make your body like the bottom stick and the sound Om like the top stick. Keep rubbing them together through meditation. Then you will see the shining God, like a spark that was hidden in the wood.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-15.plain: Oil is hidden in seeds, butter in cream, water under dry riverbeds, and fire in wood. In the same way, God is found hidden inside yourself, if you search for him with honesty and self-discipline.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-1-16.plain: God fills everything, the way butter is spread through milk. You find him through knowing yourself and through self-discipline. This is the Brahman the Upanishads teach.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-2-1.plain: This begins a prayer to Savitri, the sun god. It says Savitri first gathered his mind and thoughts, found his light, and brought fire above the earth.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-2-2.plain: With focused minds, we place ourselves under the guidance of the god Savitri so that we may find happiness.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-2-3.plain: The worshipper prays that Savitri, who reaches the gods and heaven with his mind, will help the gods make a great light shine.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-2-4.plain: The wise followers of the great sage focus their minds and thoughts. Savitri, who alone knows the right order of things, arranged the prayers. Great is the praise of Savitri.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-2-5.plain: The worshipper says the old prayer should be joined with new praise. He hopes his song will travel far like the sun's path, so that all the children of the Immortal in heaven may hear it.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-2-6.plain: Where the sacred fire is lit by rubbing, where the breath is held still, and where the sacred Soma drink flows, there the mind comes alive and becomes ready for meditation.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-1.plain: The sage Yagnavalkya had two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani. Maitreyi cared about spiritual knowledge of Brahman (the ultimate reality), while Katyayani knew only ordinary things. Yagnavalkya was ready to leave home and live as a hermit in the forest.
themes: leaving home for a spiritual life
a family at a turning point
retirement and a new stage of life

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-2.plain: Yagnavalkya tells Maitreyi that he is leaving the house for the forest. He wants to divide his property fairly between her and his other wife, Katyayani.
themes: providing for loved ones before leaving

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-3.plain: Maitreyi asks whether owning the whole rich earth would make her immortal. Yagnavalkya says no: she would live like a rich person, but money cannot give lasting life.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-4.plain: Maitreyi says she does not want things that cannot make her immortal. She asks her husband to teach her what he knows about lasting life instead.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-5.plain: Yagnavalkya is pleased by her question and says she has become even dearer to him. He agrees to explain and asks her to listen carefully.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-6.plain: Yagnavalkya teaches that we do not love a husband, wife, children, money, gods or anything else just for their own sake. We love them because of the Self, the deep inner reality in all things. So the Self is what we should look at, hear about, think about and come to know, because knowing it means knowing everything.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-7.plain: Yagnavalkya says that anyone who thinks priests, rulers, worlds, gods, scriptures or creatures exist apart from the Self will lose them. All of these, and everything, are really that one Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-8.plain: Yagnavalkya gives an example: you cannot catch the sounds of a drum by themselves. But you hold the sounds when you hold the drum or the drummer.
themes: how to know everything at once

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-9.plain: The same is true of a conch shell's sound. You cannot grab the sound alone, but you control it by holding the shell or the person blowing it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-10.plain: It is the same with a lute, a stringed instrument. You cannot grab its notes alone, but you have them when you hold the lute or the player.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-11.plain: Just as smoke rises by itself from a fire of damp wood, all the sacred books, stories, teachings, rituals, food, drink, this world, the next world and all creatures came out from the great Being like breath. Everything comes from that one source.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-12.plain: Yagnavalkya lists meeting places: all waters meet in the sea, all touches in the skin, tastes in the tongue, smells in the nose, colours in the eye, sounds in the ear, thoughts in the mind, knowledge in the heart, actions in the hands, movements in the feet, and all the Vedas in speech.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-13.plain: A lump of salt tastes salty all through, inside and out. The Self is the same: it is pure awareness through and through. It shows up through the body and elements and disappears back into them, and after death there is no more separate personal knowing.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-14.plain: Maitreyi says she is confused and does not understand. Yagnavalkya assures her he is not trying to confuse her: the Self can never be destroyed.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-5-15.plain: Yagnavalkya explains that seeing, hearing and knowing need two things: one who knows and something known. When only the Self exists, there is no other to see or know, and no one can know the Knower itself. The Self can only be described as 'not this, not this'; it cannot be grasped, cannot die, clings to nothing and does not suffer. Having taught this, he left for the forest.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-1-1.plain: That unseen reality is whole and complete, and this visible world is whole and complete too. The visible comes from the unseen, and when the whole is taken from the whole, the whole still remains. The sacred sound Om stands for Brahman, the ultimate reality, and through it one can know all that needs knowing.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-2-1.plain: The gods, humans and demons all studied under their father Prajapati, the creator. When the gods asked for a final teaching, he said only 'Da.' The gods understood it as 'Damyata,' meaning 'control yourselves,' and he agreed.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-2-2.plain: Then the humans asked for a teaching. Prajapati again said 'Da,' and they understood it as 'Datta,' meaning 'give.' He said they were right.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-2-3.plain: Then the demons asked, and Prajapati again said 'Da.' They understood it as 'Dayadhvam,' meaning 'be merciful,' and he agreed. Thunder still repeats 'Da Da Da' to remind everyone: control yourself, give, and be kind.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-3-1.plain: The heart is Prajapati, the creator; it is Brahman and everything. The word for heart, 'hridaya,' has three parts, and the passage links each to a reward: people bring offerings and gifts to the one who understands it, and he reaches heaven.
themes: the heart as the center of life

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-18.plain: Yagnavalkya continues: there is something living inside your eye that the eye itself cannot see. It uses the eye and guides it from within. That inner guide is your true Self, and it never dies.
themes: what am I beyond my body

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-19.plain: Yagnavalkya says the same about hearing. Something lives inside the ear and guides it, but the ear does not know it. That inner guide is your Self, which never dies.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-20.plain: Yagnavalkya says something lives inside your mind and guides it, yet the mind cannot know it. That inner guide is your true Self, and it is undying.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-21.plain: Yagnavalkya says something lives inside the skin, the sense of touch, and guides it from within. The skin does not know it. That inner guide is your undying Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-22.plain: Yagnavalkya says something lives inside our knowing and understanding and guides it. Our knowledge cannot grasp it. That inner guide is your true Self, which never dies.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-23.plain: Yagnavalkya says the inner guide also lives in the seed of life. It cannot be seen, heard or known, yet it is the one that sees, hears and knows in everyone. It alone is your undying Self, and everything apart from it brings suffering. After this, the sage Uddalaka Aruni, who had asked the question, fell silent.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-1.plain: Gargi, also called Vakaknavi, tells the other Brahmanas, the priests, that she will ask Yagnavalkya two questions. If he answers them, she says, none of them will beat him in debate about Brahman, the ultimate reality. Yagnavalkya invites her to ask.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-2.plain: Gargi compares herself to a warrior who strings his bow and takes two sharp arrows into battle. She says her two questions are like those arrows. Yagnavalkya calmly tells her to ask.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-3.plain: Gargi asks her first question. People say there is something above the sky, below the earth, holding both, and spanning past, present and future. What is that thing woven into, like threads on a loom?

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-4.plain: Yagnavalkya answers that all of that, across all space and all time, is woven into akasa, the space or ether that fills everything.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-5.plain: Gargi bows to Yagnavalkya for answering well. She tells him to get ready for her second question, and he says, 'Ask.'

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-6.plain: Gargi repeats her question. What is the thing that spans heaven, earth, past, present and future woven into?

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-7.plain: Yagnavalkya gives the same answer: it is woven into space, the ether. Gargi then asks the deeper question: what is space itself woven into?

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-8.plain: Yagnavalkya says the wise call the final ground the Akshara, which means 'the imperishable,' the thing that never decays. It has no size, shape, color, taste, smell or senses. It has no inside or outside. It eats nothing, and nothing can eat or destroy it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-9.plain: Yagnavalkya says everything keeps its order because of the Imperishable. Sun and moon, heaven and earth, moments, days, months and years, and rivers flowing east or west all hold their places by its command. Even people praising generous givers, and gods and ancestors receiving offerings, follow its rule.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-10.plain: Yagnavalkya says that someone who does rituals and hard spiritual practice for a thousand years without knowing the Imperishable gains only results that run out. Whoever dies without knowing it is pitiable. But whoever dies knowing it is truly wise, a true Brahmana.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-11.plain: Yagnavalkya says Brahman cannot be seen, heard or known, yet it is what sees, hears and knows. Nothing else truly sees or knows except it. Space itself is woven into this Imperishable.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-8-12.plain: Gargi tells the other priests they should feel lucky just to bow to Yagnavalkya and walk away. She says no one will beat him in debate about Brahman. Then she falls silent.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-1.plain: Next, the scholar Vidagdha Sakalya asks Yagnavalkya how many gods there are. Yagnavalkya first quotes a hymn: three hundred and three, plus three thousand and three. Each time Sakalya asks again, the number drops: thirty-three, six, three, two, one and a half, and finally one. Sakalya then asks who the thousands of gods are.
themes: searching for the one behind many

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-2.plain: Yagnavalkya says the thousands of gods are only different powers of thirty-three main gods. Those are the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Adityas, plus Indra the king of gods and Prajapati the creator.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-10.plain: The highest reality lies beyond this world. It has no shape and no suffering. People who come to know it go beyond death, while those who don't keep suffering.
themes: is there something beyond this life

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-11.plain: The Lord (Bhagavat) is present in every face, head and neck, and lives deep in the heart of every living being. Because he is everywhere, he is called Shiva, the one who is present in all places.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-12.plain: This Person (purusha, the inner spirit of all) is the great Lord. He sets everything in motion and can reach everything. He is pure light, and he never wears out or grows old.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-13.plain: The divine Person lives inside every human heart and is pictured as no bigger than a thumb. We can come to know him through our heart, thoughts and mind. Those who truly know him go beyond death.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-14.plain: This verse pictures the divine Person as having a thousand heads, eyes and feet. He wraps around the whole earth and still reaches beyond it.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-15.plain: The divine Person is everything that exists: all that has been and all that will be. He rules over eternal life, and he is also every living thing that grows by eating food.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-16.plain: The divine reality has hands, feet, eyes, heads and ears everywhere. It surrounds and holds everything in the world.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-17.plain: The divine reality has no senses of its own, yet it shines through the work of all our senses. It is the ruler of all, and the safe place where everyone can turn for shelter.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-18.plain: The spirit lives in the body, which is like a town with nine gates. Like a bird, it flutters outward into the world. This same spirit rules the whole world, everything that stays still and everything that moves.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-19.plain: The divine Person grasps without hands, moves fast without feet, sees without eyes and hears without ears. He knows everything that can be known, but no one fully knows him. He is called the first, the great Person.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-20.plain: The Self is smaller than the smallest thing and greater than the greatest, and it hides in the heart of every creature. A person who has let go of all sorrow sees this glorious, calm Lord, and this happens through the Lord's own grace.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-3-21.plain: The speaker says he knows this ancient one who never grows old, the Self of all things, endless and everywhere. Teachers of sacred knowledge say he is eternal, and that in him the cycle of being born again comes to an end.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-1.plain: God is like the sun, which has no color itself yet brings out endless colors. With his power (shakti) and on purpose, he makes the world. Everything comes from him at the start and returns to him at the end. The verse prays that he will give us good thoughts.
themes: where did the world come from

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-2.plain: The one Self is fire, the sun, the wind and the moon. It is the starry sky, the water, and the creator gods. All these are really that one reality.
themes: seeing the divine in the world

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-3.plain: Speaking to God, the verse says: you are woman and man, young boy and young girl. You are the old man walking slowly with a stick. You are born facing every direction.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-4.plain: Speaking to God, the verse says: you are the dark-blue bee and the green parrot with red eyes. You are the storm cloud, the seasons and the seas. You have no beginning because you are endless, and all worlds are born from you.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-5.plain: This riddle speaks of one unborn female being, red, white and black, who is all of one kind yet gives birth to many offspring. One unborn male being loves her and lies beside her. Another one leaves her while she is busy eating what is there to be eaten.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-6.plain: Two birds, close friends who never part, sit on the same tree. One eats the sweet fruit. The other just watches and does not eat.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-7.plain: A person sitting on that same tree feels sad, confused and lost because he feels powerless. But when he sees the other one, the Lord, who is calm and content, and knows his greatness, his sadness goes away.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-8.plain: What good is the Rig Veda to someone who does not know the eternal, sky-like Self it speaks of, the highest one in whom all the gods live? Only those who know this Self find real contentment.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-4.plain: King Janaka (Ganaka Vaideha) asks the sage Yajnavalkya what lights a person's way once both the sun and the moon have set. Yajnavalkya answers that fire is then the light that lets a person sit, move about, work and come home.
themes: what guides us in the dark

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-5.plain: The king asks what a person's light is when the sun, moon and fire are all gone. Yajnavalkya says sound is then the light: even when you cannot see your own hand in the dark, you can walk toward a voice.
themes: finding your way when you can't see

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-6.plain: The king asks what light is left when the sun, moon, fire and even sound are all gone. Yajnavalkya answers that the Self, a person's own inner being, is the light by which they live and act.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-7.plain: The king asks who this Self is. Yajnavalkya says it is the bright, knowing presence inside the heart, surrounded by the senses. It stays the same while it moves between this world and the dream world, and in dreams it goes beyond everything that dies.
themes: the part of us that doesn't change

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-8.plain: When the Self is born and takes on a body, it becomes tied up with all kinds of troubles and wrongs. When the body dies, the Self leaves all those troubles behind.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-9.plain: Yajnavalkya says a person has two places, this world and the next world, plus an in-between state, dreaming sleep, where both can be glimpsed. In dreams the person takes pieces of the waking world, breaks them down and builds them up again, lit only by their own inner light.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-10.plain: In dreams there are no real chariots, horses, roads, lakes or rivers, and no real joys. The dreamer makes all of them up. The Self is the maker of the dream world.
themes: the mind creates its own world

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-11.plain: An old verse says that in sleep the Self quiets the body and senses but does not sleep itself. It watches over them, and then returns to its place, shining like a golden person or a lonely bird.
themes: the part of us that stays awake

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-12.plain: While breath keeps the body, the 'lower nest', alive, the deathless Self flies out of it and goes wherever it likes in dreams, like a golden, lonely bird.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-13.plain: In dreams the Self goes up and down and takes many shapes. It might enjoy love, laugh with friends, or see frightening things.
themes: the mind creates its own world

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-14.plain: People can see the dream world, but no one ever sees the Self that makes it, so you should not wake a sleeper suddenly in case it does not return to the body properly. Some people say dreams only repeat what we see while awake, but Yajnavalkya says the dreamer shines by its own light. The grateful king gives him a thousand and asks him to keep teaching so he can become free.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-15.plain: After enjoying deep, peaceful sleep and seeing good and bad, the Self goes back to dreaming. Nothing it saw clings to it, because the Self is not attached to anything. The king again gives a thousand and asks him to go on.
themes: letting go of what we've seen

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-16.plain: After roaming in dreams and seeing good and bad, the Self returns to being awake. What it saw in the dream does not cling to it, because it is attached to nothing. The king once more rewards Yajnavalkya and asks for more.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-17.plain: After living through the waking day and seeing good and bad, the Self goes back again into dreaming sleep.
themes: the cycle of day and night

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-18.plain: A large fish swims along both banks of a river, the right and the left. In the same way, the Self moves back and forth between dreaming and waking.
themes: the part of us that doesn't change

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-19.plain: A falcon gets tired after flying around, folds its wings and heads home to its nest. In the same way, the Self hurries into deep sleep, where it wants nothing and dreams nothing.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-20.plain: The body has tiny channels called Hita, finer than a hair and full of colors. In dreams, out of ignorance, a person may imagine being killed, chased by an elephant or falling into a well, the same dangers feared while awake. But when he feels he is a god or a king, or that he is everything, that is his highest state.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-21.plain: In deep sleep a person shows their true nature: free of wanting, free of wrong, free of fear. Just as someone held by a loved one forgets everything inside and outside, the person held by the knowing Self is aware of nothing else. There every wish is fulfilled, no wish is left, and there is no sorrow.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-22.plain: In that state, labels no longer apply. Father and mother, gods and holy books, thief and murderer, outcaste groups like Chandalas and Paulkasas, and wandering monks and hermits all stop being what they were. Neither good nor bad deeds follow the person, and every sorrow of the heart is gone.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-23.plain: People say that in deep sleep a person sees nothing. Yet the power to see is still there, because the seer can never be destroyed. There is simply nothing separate from him to look at.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-23.plain: Sakalya asks Yagnavalkya which god rules the north. Yagnavalkya says Soma, the moon and sacred drink. Soma rests on the Diksha (a vow taken before a ritual), the vow rests on truth, and truth rests in the heart, because we know what is true with our heart.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-24.plain: Sakalya asks about the god of the sky above. Yagnavalkya says Agni, the fire god, who rests in speech, and speech rests in the heart. Then Sakalya presses further and asks what the heart itself rests on.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-25.plain: Yagnavalkya calls Sakalya a fool (Ahallika) for thinking the heart could rest somewhere outside us. If the heart were away from the body, he says, dogs or birds could eat it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-26.plain: Yagnavalkya says body and self rest on the breath, and he names the five kinds of breath in a chain. The true Self can only be described as "not this, not this": it cannot be grasped, cannot die, clings to nothing, and does not suffer. He then asks Sakalya to explain the Self taught in the Upanishads. Sakalya cannot, and as warned, his head falls off.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-27.plain: After Sakalya's death, Yagnavalkya invites all the priests to question him, one by one or all together, or to be questioned by him. None of them dares to speak.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-28.plain: Yagnavalkya compares a person to a tree: hair like leaves, skin like bark, blood like sap, bones like hard wood. A cut tree grows again from its root, but what root makes a person live again after death? The answer given is Brahman, the highest reality, which is knowledge and joy. It is the final support both for the one who gives to others and for the one who stands firm in knowing.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-1.plain: King Janaka of Videha is holding court when Yagnavalkya arrives. The king asks if he came for cows as a reward or for deep questions. Yagnavalkya says he came for both.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-2.plain: Janaka says a teacher told him speech is Brahman, the highest reality. Yagnavalkya agrees but says that teaching stands on only one leg, so it is incomplete. He adds that the tongue is its body and space is its home, and that it should be honored as knowledge, since through speech we know friends, holy books and the world. The king offers a thousand cows, but Yagnavalkya refuses payment until the teaching is complete.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-3.plain: Janaka says another teacher told him life-breath (prana) is Brahman. Yagnavalkya says breath is its body and space its home, and it should be honored as what is dear. Life is so dear that people will do unworthy things or travel into danger to protect it. Again he refuses the reward until the teaching is complete.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-4.plain: Janaka says a teacher told him sight is Brahman. Yagnavalkya says the eye is its body and space its home, and it should be honored as truth, because when someone says "I saw it," people believe it. He refuses payment until the teaching is complete.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-5.plain: Janaka says a teacher told him hearing is Brahman. Yagnavalkya says the ear is its body and space its home, and it should be honored as endless, because the directions of space never come to an end, and hearing is linked to space. He refuses payment until the teaching is complete.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-6.plain: Janaka says Satyakama Jabala told him the mind is Brahman. Yagnavalkya says the mind is its body and space its home, and it should be honored as joy. Through the mind a man desires a wife, and the son born to them is a joy. He refuses payment until the teaching is complete.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-1-7.plain: Janaka says Sakalya told him the heart is Brahman. Yagnavalkya says the heart is its body and space its home, and it should be honored as steadiness, because all things rest in the heart. Once more he refuses payment until the teaching is complete.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-2-1.plain: King Janaka steps down from his throne, bows, and asks Yagnavalkya to teach him. Yagnavalkya says the king is well prepared with learning, like a traveler with a chariot. Then he asks where the king will go when he dies. Janaka admits he does not know, and Yagnavalkya promises to tell him.
themes: where do we go after death

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-2-2.plain: Yagnavalkya says the person seen in the right eye is called Indha, "the shining one." People call him Indra, king of the gods, as a hidden name, because the gods like hidden names more than plain ones.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-2-3.plain: Yagnavalkya says the figure in the right eye is Indra's wife, Viraj. They meet in the space inside the heart and are fed there. They travel along a channel rising up from the heart. Tiny veins called Hita, finer than a hair split a thousand ways, carry finer food to the inner self (the Taigasa).
themes: the inner life of the body
what happens in sleep and dreams
the heart as a meeting place

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-2-4.plain: Yagnavalkya says all the directions are the breaths going out to them. The Self can only be described as "not this, not this": it cannot be grasped, does not decay, clings to nothing, does not suffer or die. He tells Janaka he has reached fearlessness. The grateful king wishes him the same and offers him his whole kingdom and himself.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-1.plain: Yagnavalkya comes to King Janaka planning to stay quiet. But long ago, after a debate about the fire ritual (Agnihotra), he had granted the king the right to ask any question he liked. So the king asks first.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-2.plain: Janaka asks what gives a person light. Yagnavalkya says the sun, because by its light we sit, move, work and come home. The king agrees.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-3.plain: Janaka asks what gives a person light after the sun has set. Yagnavalkya says the moon, because by its light we can still sit, move, work and come home. The king agrees.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-9.plain: The scholar Gargya says he worships the person seen in a mirror as Brahman, the ultimate reality. King Agatasatru stops him and says he already honors that as "the brilliant." Whoever honors it this way becomes brilliant, and so do his children, and he outshines the people he meets.
themes: mistaking a reflection for the real self

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-10.plain: Gargya says he worships the sound that follows a person as they walk as Brahman. Agatasatru says he already honors that as "life." Whoever honors it this way lives a full lifespan, and breath does not leave him too early.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-11.plain: Gargya says he worships the person in space as Brahman. Agatasatru says he already honors that as "the companion who never leaves us." Whoever honors it this way always has a companion, and his group of friends and followers is never cut off from him.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-12.plain: Gargya says he worships the person made of shadow as Brahman. Agatasatru says he already honors that as "death." Whoever honors it this way lives his whole lifespan, and death does not come to him before its time.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-13.plain: Gargya says he worships the person in the body as Brahman. Agatasatru says he already honors that as "the embodied one." Whoever honors it this way becomes embodied, and so do his children. Then Gargya has nothing more to say and falls silent.
themes: is the self just the body

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-14.plain: Agatasatru asks Gargya if that is all he knows, and Gargya admits it is. The king says this is not enough to truly know Brahman. Gargya humbly asks to become the king's student.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-15.plain: Agatasatru says it is unusual for a Brahmin, a priest and teacher, to ask a Kshatriya, a warrior-king, to teach him about Brahman, but he agrees to explain it clearly. He takes Gargya by the hand to a sleeping man and calls out grand names to him, but the man does not wake. Only when the king shakes him does he get up.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-16.plain: Agatasatru asks Gargya where the man's conscious self was while he was asleep, and where it came back from when he woke up. Gargya does not know the answer.
themes: where do we go when we sleep

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-17.plain: Agatasatru explains that during sleep, the knowing self gathers in the powers of all the senses and rests in the space inside the heart. Then breath, speech, hearing, sight and mind are all drawn inward. This drawing in is what we call sleep.
themes: where the mind goes at night

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-18.plain: Agatasatru explains that when a person dreams, the dream becomes his world. In it he may seem to be a great king or a great priest, or seem to rise and fall. Like a king moving freely around his own kingdom, the self takes the senses with it and moves as it likes within its own body.
themes: the mind creating its own world

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-19.plain: Agatasatru explains that in deep, dreamless sleep, when a person knows nothing, the self moves through 72,000 channels called Hita that spread from the heart through the body, and rests there. It rests as peacefully as a young man or a great king at the height of happiness.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-20.plain: Agatasatru teaches that just as a spider spins out its thread and sparks fly up from a fire, all senses, worlds, gods and living beings come out of the Self. The Self's secret name is "the Truth of the truth": the senses are real, but the Self is even more real than they are.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-2-1.plain: This riddle speaks of a baby with its home, room, post and rope. The baby is the inner life, the home is the body, the room is the head, the post is the breath, and the rope is food. Whoever understands this keeps away seven hostile forces.
themes: the body as a home for life

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-2-2.plain: The passage links each part of the eye to a god: the red lines to Rudra, the tears to Parjanya the rain god, the pupil to the sun, the iris to Agni the fire god, the white to Indra, and the eyelashes to earth and heaven. Whoever knows this will never run short of food.
themes: the divine in the human body
seeing the sacred in ordinary things

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-2-3.plain: A verse describes an upside-down cup filled with glory, with seven sages on its rim and a tongue as the eighth that speaks with Brahman. The passage explains that the cup is the head, the glory and the sages are the senses, and the tongue, through speech, connects with the divine.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-2-4.plain: The passage names the senses after famous sages called Rishis: the two ears, two eyes and two nostrils each match a pair of sages, and the tongue is the sage Atri, whose name sounds like the word for eating. Whoever knows this can enjoy everything as his food.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-3-1.plain: Brahman, the ultimate reality, has two forms. One has shape, dies and is solid. The other has no shape, never dies and is flowing. Together they make up what is called "true."

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-3-2.plain: Everything except the wind and the sky has a shape, will die, and is solid and fixed. The shining sun is the very essence of all these solid, mortal things.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-3-3.plain: The wind and the sky have no fixed shape, do not die, and flow freely. The essence of these unseen things is the person inside the sun's disk. This is how it works in the world of nature and the gods.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-3-4.plain: Now the same teaching is applied to the human body. Everything in the body except the breath and the space inside it is solid, mortal and fixed. The eye is the essence of these solid parts.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-9.plain: God, the maker, brings out everything from himself: the holy verses, the rituals, the past and the future, and all that the Vedas (the oldest sacred books of India) speak of. The individual soul gets tangled up in this world through maya, God's creative power that makes the world appear.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-10.plain: Nature (Prakriti) is like the maker's art or magic (Maya), and the great Lord is the maker. The whole world is filled with parts of him.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-11.plain: There is one God who rules over every cause, in whom everything comes together and comes apart again. He gives blessings and is worthy of worship. A person who truly sees him enters lasting peace.
themes: things coming together and falling apart

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-12.plain: This is a prayer to Rudra, a name for God, who creates and supports the gods. He is the great seer who watched Hiranyagarbha, the first created being, be born. The prayer asks him to give us good thoughts.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-13.plain: God is the ruler of the gods. All the worlds rest in him, and he rules over all creatures with two feet and four feet. The speakers say: let us offer our worship to him.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-14.plain: God is finer and more hidden than the smallest thing. He creates everything in the middle of chaos, takes many forms, and surrounds all things. He is called Shiva, "the kind one." Whoever knows him gains peace forever.
themes: peace in the middle of chaos

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-15.plain: God has always guarded this world. He is the lord of all and hides inside every living being. The great sages and the gods are joined in him. Whoever knows him breaks free from the chains of death.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-16.plain: Shiva, the blessed God, is hidden in all beings. He is like the thin, rich layer that rises to the top of clarified butter, and he surrounds everything. Whoever knows this God is set free from everything that binds him.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-17.plain: God, the maker of all, the great Self, always lives in a person's heart. He is known through the heart, the soul and the mind. Those who know him become immortal.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-18.plain: When this inner light rises, there is no day or night, and no being or not-being. Only Shiva, the blessed one, is there. This is the eternal, holy light of Savitri, the sun god, and the ancient wisdom came from it.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-19.plain: No one can grasp God from above, from the side or in the middle. There is no picture or likeness of him. His name is Great Glory.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-20.plain: God's form cannot be seen, and no eye can see him. But people who know him with heart and mind, living in their heart, become immortal.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-21.plain: A worshipper comes to God trembling and says, "You were never born." He prays, "O Rudra, let your kind face protect me forever."

upanishads-shvetashvatara-4-22.plain: The worshippers pray to Rudra, who could be fierce, not to harm their children, grandchildren, their own lives, their cows or their horses. They ask him not to kill their men in anger, since they always call on him with offerings.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-1.plain: In the highest Brahman, the endless and undying reality, both knowledge and ignorance are hidden. Ignorance passes away, but knowledge lasts forever. The one who rules over both is someone else: God.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-2.plain: The one God rules over every cause and every form. In the beginning he held in his thoughts the wise, fiery son, and he wished to watch him as he was born.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-3.plain: God spreads out the world like a net again and again in many ways, and then draws it back in. The great Lord also created other rulers, and he rules over all of them.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-4.plain: The sun lights up every direction: above, below and across. In the same way, the one holy God rules over everything that can grow from a seed.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-5.plain: The one God rules over everything. Because of him, the seed of the universe grows into its true nature. He makes all things different and decides all their qualities.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-6.plain: This truth is hidden in the Upanishads, which are hidden inside the Vedas. Brahma, the first created being, knows it as the seed of all. The ancient gods and poets who knew it became one with it and became immortal.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-5.plain: Some teachers teach the sacred Savitri prayer in a different verse form called Anushtubh, claiming it stands for speech. The Upanishad says not to do this, but to teach it as the Gayatri. Even a large payment given to a teacher who knows this is worth less than one part of the Gayatri.
themes: doing sacred practice the right way

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-6.plain: Even if a teacher were paid with the three worlds, all the knowledge of the Vedas (the holy scriptures), and every living thing, that would only equal the first three parts of the Gayatri prayer. Its fourth, shining part is beyond anything anyone can own, so no payment could ever match it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-7.plain: This is a prayer of praise to the Gayatri: it has one, two, three and four parts, yet it has no parts because it cannot be fully known. Bow to its fourth shining part beyond the skies. A person who knows this can use the prayer to block the wishes of someone he dislikes, or to gain what he himself wants.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-8.plain: King Janaka of Videha teased the scholar Budila, who claimed to know the Gayatri, asking why he had been reborn as an elephant carrying the king. Budila said he had not known the prayer's 'mouth,' which is fire. Just as fire burns up any amount of wood, a person who truly knows this burns up even great wrongs and becomes pure and free from death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-15-1.plain: A prayer: the face of the highest Truth is hidden behind a golden disk, like the sun. It asks Pushan, the god who nourishes and guides, to remove that cover so we can see what is truly real.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-15-2.plain: The prayer calls the sun by many names, including Pushan, the lone seer, Yama the judge, and Surya, son of Prajapati. It asks the sun to spread out its rays and gather them in. The worshipper says he sees its most beautiful light, and declares, 'I am that same being who lives in the sun.'
themes: prayer at the end of life

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-15-3.plain: A dying person prays that his breath may return to the air and the deathless, as his body becomes ashes. He tells his own mind to remember the deeds he has done in his life.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-15-4.plain: A prayer to Agni, the god of fire, who knows everything. It asks him to lead us by a good road to true happiness, to keep crooked wrongdoing far away, and promises him our fullest praise.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-1.plain: Breath is the first and best of the powers in the body. Whoever understands this becomes first and best among his people, and among whomever he chooses.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-2.plain: Speech is called the richest of the body's powers. Whoever understands this becomes the richest among his people.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-3.plain: The eye is the firm support, because seeing lets a person stand steady on smooth or rough ground. Whoever understands this stands firm on smooth and rough ground.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-4.plain: The ear is success, because the holy Vedas are learned by hearing them. Whoever understands this gets whatever he wishes for.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-5.plain: The mind is the home where everything rests. Whoever understands this becomes a home, a place of support, for his own people and for everyone.
themes: the mind as a resting place

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-6.plain: Seed, the power to create new life, is called generation. Whoever understands this has many children and much cattle.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-7.plain: The body's powers, called Pranas here, argued about which of them was the best and asked Brahman, the Creator. He said the best is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off.
themes: arguing over who is most important

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-8.plain: Speech left the body for a year to test the others. When it came back, they said they lived fine like people who cannot speak, still breathing, seeing, hearing and thinking. So speech came back in.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-9.plain: Then sight left for a year. The others lived on like blind people, still breathing, speaking, hearing and thinking. So the eye came back in.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-10.plain: Then hearing left for a year. The others lived on like deaf people, still breathing, speaking, seeing and thinking. So the ear came back in.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-11.plain: Then the mind left for a year. The others lived on like foolish people who do not understand, but still breathing, seeing and hearing. So the mind came back in.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-6-1-12.plain: Then the seed, the power to have children, left for a year. The others lived on like people unable to have children, still breathing, seeing, hearing and thinking. So the seed came back in.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-4-3.plain: A teacher prays to Om, the sacred sound, calling it a treasure. He asks to be honored among people and richer than the richest, to become one with Om and be made clean by it, and for students to come to him as steadily as water flows downhill. He ends by asking Om to be his shelter, to give him understanding and to take hold of him completely.
themes: wanting to be a good teacher

upanishads-taittiriya-1-5-1.plain: Bhu, Bhuvas and Suvas are three sacred words spoken in prayer. A sage named Mahakamasya added a fourth word, Mahas, and said it stands for Brahman, the one reality behind everything, and the other three are like its limbs. Bhu stands for this earth, Bhuvas for the sky, and Suvas for the heavenly world.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-5-2.plain: The fourth word, Mahas, is linked to the sun, because the sun makes all the worlds grow. In another set, Bhu is fire, Bhuvas is air and Suvas is the sun, while Mahas is the moon, which makes all the lights in the sky shine brighter. In a third set, the three words stand for the three kinds of Vedic verses: Rik, Saman and Yajus.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-5-3.plain: Mahas is Brahman, the ultimate reality, and it makes all the Vedas, the sacred texts, great. The three other words stand for three kinds of breath in the body, and Mahas is food, which keeps all breathing going. Whoever understands these four groups of four knows Brahman, and all the gods honor that person.
themes: seeing the sacred in the body

upanishads-taittiriya-1-6-1.plain: Inside the heart there is a small space, and in it lives a Person made of mind who is shining, golden and cannot die. The soft flap at the back of the throat is called the starting point of Indra, the lord. Where the hair parts on the head, he opens the two sides of the head and, saying the sacred word Bhu, enters fire, and saying Bhuvas, enters the air.
themes: the body as a sacred path

upanishads-taittiriya-1-6-2.plain: Saying Suvas, the knower enters the sun, and saying Mahas, he enters Brahman, the ultimate reality. There he becomes master of his own mind, speech, sight, hearing and understanding. He reaches Brahman, which is like open space, true, joyful in life and mind, perfectly peaceful and undying. The teacher tells his student Prachinayogya to meditate on Brahman this way.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-7-1.plain: The text lists things in the world in groups of five, like earth, sky, heaven and the directions, or fire, air, sun, moon and stars. It also lists the body in groups of five, like five kinds of breath, five senses, and skin, flesh, muscle, bone and marrow. A sage concluded that everything comes in fives, and that the fives inside the body match and complete the fives outside it.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-1.plain: The sacred sound Om stands for Brahman, the one ultimate reality.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-2.plain: Om stands for everything that exists.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-3.plain: Om is also a word of agreement, like saying "yes." When people are told "Om, speak," they begin to speak.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-4.plain: Priests say Om before they sing the Saman chants.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-5.plain: Priests say Om before they recite the sacred hymns.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-6.plain: The Adhvaryu, the priest who handles the ritual actions, says Om before he gives his reply in the ceremony.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-7.plain: The chief priest, who oversees the ritual, says Om before he gives instructions.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-8.plain: The person holding the ceremony says Om to give permission for the Agnihotra, the daily fire offering.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-8-9.plain: When a Brahmin, a priest-teacher, begins to recite or teach, he says, "Om, may I gain the Veda," the sacred knowledge. By doing this, he truly gains it.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-9-1.plain: The text says each good duty must go together with learning and practising the Veda, the sacred texts. These duties include doing right, being truthful, self-discipline, self-control, calm, keeping the sacred fires and offerings, welcoming guests, doing one's duty, marriage, children and grandchildren. Three teachers each pick one thing as most important: one says truth, one says self-discipline, and one says learning and practising the Veda, because that itself is self-discipline.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-10-1.plain: The speaker says, "I am the one who shakes the tree," meaning the tree of the world, which has to be cut down by knowledge.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-10-2.plain: The speaker says his glory is like the top of a mountain, high and lofty.

upanishads-taittiriya-1-10-3.plain: The speaker says the pure light of his knowledge has risen high. He is the same undying reality that lives in the sun.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-3.plain: Sakalya asks who the Vasus are. Yagnavalkya says they are fire, earth, air, sky, sun, heaven, moon and stars. They are called Vasus, meaning "dwellers," because everything in the world lives and rests in them.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-4.plain: Yagnavalkya says the Rudras are the ten life-powers of the body: the five senses and the five powers of action, with the self as the eleventh. When they leave the body at death, they make the living cry. The word Rudra comes from "to make cry."
themes: why we cry when someone dies

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-5.plain: Yagnavalkya says the Adityas are the twelve months of the year. They are called Adityas because they keep moving on and take everything along with them.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-6.plain: Yagnavalkya says Indra, king of the gods, is thunder, which means the thunderbolt. Pragapati, the lord of creatures, is the sacrifice, which means the animals offered in it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-7.plain: Yagnavalkya names the six gods: fire, earth, air, sky, sun and heaven. Together these six make up the whole world.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-8.plain: Yagnavalkya says the three gods are the three worlds, because all the gods live in them. The two gods are food and breath. The "one and a half" god is the wind that blows.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-9.plain: People ask why the wind, which is one, is called "one and a half." The answer is a word-play: when the wind blows, everything grows. Finally Yagnavalkya says the one god is breath, which is Brahman, the thread running through all things, and people simply call it "That."

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-10.plain: Sakalya says a real teacher must know the being whose home is the earth and the body. Yagnavalkya says he knows it: it is the physical person, the body. He asks Sakalya what deity rules it, and Sakalya answers, "The Immortal."

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-11.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is desire and love. Yagnavalkya says it is the loving person, the self full of desire. Sakalya says its deity is women.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-12.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is colours and whose seeing is the eye. Yagnavalkya says it is the person in the sun. Sakalya says its deity is the True.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-13.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is open space and whose sense is the ear. Yagnavalkya says it is the person who hears and answers. Sakalya says its deity is Space.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-14.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is darkness. Yagnavalkya says it is the shadow person. Sakalya says its deity is Death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-15.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is bright colours and whose sense is the eye. Yagnavalkya says it is the person seen in a mirror. Sakalya says its deity is the breath of life.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-16.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is water. Yagnavalkya says it is the person in the water. Sakalya says its deity is Varuna, the god of the waters.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-17.plain: Sakalya asks about the being whose home is seed. Yagnavalkya says it is the son, the person born from a parent. Sakalya says its deity is Pragapati, the lord of creatures.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-18.plain: Yagnavalkya asks Sakalya if the other priests, who were too afraid to argue, pushed him forward to be beaten. Sakalya angrily asks what Brahman Yagnavalkya knows, since he looked down on the priests of the Kuru-Panchala lands.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-19.plain: Yagnavalkya says he knows the directions of the world, their gods, and where those gods rest. Sakalya begins to test him on this.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-20.plain: For the east, Yagnavalkya names the sun. The sun rests in the eye, the eye rests in the colours it sees, and the colours rest in the heart, because we know what we see through the heart. Sakalya agrees.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-21.plain: For the south, Yagnavalkya names Yama, god of death. Yama rests in sacrifice, sacrifice rests in the gifts given to priests, and the gifts rest in faith, because only a person who believes gives. Faith rests in the heart, because the heart is how we know faith. Sakalya agrees.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-9-22.plain: For the west, Yagnavalkya names Varuna, god of waters. Varuna rests in water, water in seed, and seed in the heart. That is why people say a son who looks like his father came from his father's heart. Sakalya agrees.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-4-1.plain: The heart spoken of before is the true Brahman, the ultimate reality behind everything. Whoever knows this great first-born reality as the truth wins these worlds and overcomes his enemies, because Brahman is truth itself.
themes: truth as the foundation of life

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-5-1.plain: At the start the world was water, and from it came truth, which is Brahman, the ultimate reality. Brahman produced Prajapati, the creator, who produced the gods, and the gods honor only truth. The word for truth, satyam, has three parts; the outer two stand for truth and the middle for untruth, so truth surrounds untruth and is stronger, and untruth cannot harm one who knows this.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-5-2.plain: The truth is the sun, the being who lives in the sun, and the being in a person's right eye. They support each other: the sun shines its rays into the eye, and the eye's senses reach out to the sun. When a person is about to die, he sees the sun as plain white, and its rays no longer come back to him.
themes: our link to the sun and nature

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-5-3.plain: The being in the sun is pictured using three sacred words: Bhuh is his head, Bhuvah his two arms, and Svar his two feet, matching the number of syllables. His secret name is Ahar, meaning 'day.' Whoever knows this destroys evil and leaves it behind.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-5-4.plain: The being in the right eye is pictured the same way: Bhuh is his head, Bhuvah his two arms, and Svar his feet. His secret name is Aham, meaning 'I.' Whoever knows this destroys evil and leaves it behind.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-6-1.plain: Inside the heart lives a being made of mind and light, as tiny as a grain of rice or barley. Yet this small being is the ruler and lord of everything that exists.
themes: who is in charge of the world

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-7-1.plain: People say lightning is Brahman, the ultimate reality, because the word for lightning comes from the idea of 'cutting.' Whoever knows this is cut free from evil by Brahman.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-8-1.plain: One should think of speech as a cow with four udders, which are four sacred words used in rituals. The gods are fed by two of them, people by one, and the ancestors by the last. Breath is the cow's bull and the mind is her calf.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-9-1.plain: There is a fire inside each person, called Agni Vaishvanara, that digests the food we eat. It is the humming sound you hear when you cover your ears. When someone is about to die, they no longer hear it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-10-1.plain: When a person dies, he goes first to the wind, which opens a small gap for him to rise through. Then the sun and the moon each open a gap, and he rises past them. He reaches a world with no sorrow and no cold, and lives there for endless years.
themes: hope for a loved one who died

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-11-1.plain: When a sick person suffers pain, that suffering counts as the highest spiritual discipline. Being carried to the forest after death, and being placed on the funeral fire, also count as the highest discipline. Whoever understands this wins the highest world.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-12-1.plain: Some say food is Brahman, the ultimate reality, and others say life-breath is, but each fails without the other, so some say they are highest when joined. Pratrida asks his father whether he could do any good or harm to someone who knows this. His father waves his hand and says no, because knowing only that these two are one does not reach the highest state. Then he teaches that food is 'Vi' because all beings rest on it, and life is 'Ram' because all beings delight in it. All beings rest on and delight in the one who knows this.
themes: body and life need each other

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-13-1.plain: Breath is the Uktha, a sacred hymn, because breath raises everything up. Whoever knows this will have a wise son and becomes one with the Uktha.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-13-2.plain: Breath is the Yajus, the ritual verses, because all beings are joined together through breath. For one who knows this, all beings join to help him do well, and he becomes one with the Yajus.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-13-3.plain: Breath is the Saman, the sung chants, because all beings meet in breath. For one who knows this, all beings come together to help him do well, and he becomes one with the Saman.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-13-4.plain: Breath is Kshatra, meaning power and protection, because breath protects a person from harm. Whoever knows this gains a power that needs no protection and becomes one with it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-1.plain: The words for earth, sky and heaven together make eight syllables, just like the first line of the Gayatri, a sacred verse. Whoever knows this line as the three worlds wins everything those worlds contain.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-2.plain: The names of the three Vedas, the oldest holy books, together make eight syllables, like the second line of the Gayatri. Whoever knows this line as the three Vedas gains all that this sacred knowledge reaches.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-3.plain: The names of three kinds of breath make eight syllables, like the third line of the Gayatri, and whoever knows this gains all that breathes. The Gayatri also has a fourth, shining part high above the skies, meaning the being seen in the sun. Whoever knows this fourth part shines with happiness and glory.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-5-14-4.plain: The Gayatri rests on its shining fourth part, which rests on truth, and truth is the eye, which is why we trust someone who says 'I saw' over someone who says 'I heard.' Truth in turn rests on strength, which is life-breath. The Gayatri is named for protecting the life-breaths, and a teacher who teaches it protects the life of his student.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-7.plain: The individual soul takes on qualities and does actions that bring results. It enjoys or suffers what it has done, and so it moves from life to life in many forms. It is driven by the three Gunas (the basic qualities of nature: calm, restless and dull) and travels the three paths of different rebirths.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-8.plain: This individual soul is described as no bigger than a thumb, yet bright like the sun. It has a sense of 'I', thoughts, a mind and a body. It can also seem as tiny as the point of an animal driver's stick.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-9.plain: The living soul is unimaginably tiny, like a hair's tip split into a hundred parts and then split a hundred times again. Yet the same soul is also infinite.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-10.plain: The soul is not female, not male, and not neither. It only seems to be one of these because of the body it is joined to.
themes: we are more than our bodies

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-11.plain: Through thoughts, touch, sight and desires, the soul takes on different bodies in different places, one after another, according to its deeds. It is like how a body grows from the food and drink it takes in.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-12.plain: The soul takes on many bodies, heavy or subtle, according to its own qualities. Because of its actions and its bodies, it appears as one being and then another.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-13.plain: God has no beginning and no end. He creates everything in the middle of chaos, takes many forms and surrounds all things. Whoever truly knows him is set free from every bondage.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-5-14.plain: God can be grasped by the mind, but he is not the body, which is just a 'nest'. He is Shiva, the happy one, who makes what exists and what does not, and creates the elements. Those who know him have left the body behind.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-1.plain: Some thinkers are confused and say that Nature or Time causes everything. But it is God's greatness that keeps the great wheel of the universe turning.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-2.plain: God always surrounds this world. He knows everything and is the master even of time. At his command creation unfolds as earth, water, fire, air and space.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-3.plain: After creating and then resting, God joins the soul with matter. He combines them with one, two, three or eight things, and with time and the subtle powers of the mind. The sentence continues in the next verse.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-4.plain: God starts all actions made of the three qualities of nature and puts everything in order. When it all ends and is destroyed, he goes on, because he is truly different from everything he made.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-5.plain: God is the beginning and causes the soul to be joined to the body. He is beyond past, present and future, and he is whole, without parts. We see him this way after we first worship him, the source of all, as living in our own mind.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-6.plain: God is beyond the world, which is like a great tree, and beyond time, yet the world turns because of him. He brings good and removes evil. He is the lord of joy, deathless and the support of all, and he can be known as living within oneself.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-7.plain: Let us come to know God, the greatest lord of all lords, the highest of all gods, the master of all masters, the ruler of the world, who is worthy of worship.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-8.plain: Nothing is known that God produces as an effect, and nothing caused him. No one is equal to him or greater. His high power shows itself in many ways, and his strength and knowledge are part of his very nature.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-9.plain: No one in the world is God's master or ruler, and no mark can show him. He is the cause of everything and the lord of all the senses. He has no parent and no lord.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-10.plain: Like a spider covering itself with its own threads, the one God covers himself with the world he draws out of nature. The speaker prays that this God will let us enter Brahman, the ultimate reality.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-11.plain: There is one God hidden in every living being. He is everywhere and is the inner self of all beings. He watches all actions and is the silent witness, untouched by any qualities.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-12.plain: God is the one ruler behind many things that seem to act on their own but really do not. He turns one seed into many things. Wise people who find him within themselves have lasting happiness, and no one else does.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-24.plain: The sage Yajnavalkya explains that in deep, dreamless sleep (Sushupti) a person does not smell anything. Yet the power of smelling is still there and never dies. There is simply nothing separate from him left to smell.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-25.plain: In deep, dreamless sleep a person tastes nothing. Still, the power to taste does not disappear. There is just nothing outside him to taste.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-26.plain: In deep, dreamless sleep a person says nothing. Still, the power to speak is not destroyed. There is simply no one else there to speak to.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-27.plain: In deep, dreamless sleep a person hears nothing. Still, the power to hear stays and cannot perish. There is just no second thing there for him to hear.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-28.plain: In deep, dreamless sleep a person has no thoughts. Still, the one who thinks is still there and cannot be destroyed. There is simply nothing separate from him to think about.
themes: who am I beyond my thoughts

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-29.plain: In deep, dreamless sleep a person touches nothing. Still, the power to feel touch does not die. There is just nothing outside him to touch.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-30.plain: In deep, dreamless sleep a person does not know any object. Still, the knower is there and cannot perish. There is simply nothing separate from him to know.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-31.plain: When we are awake or dreaming, there seems to be something else besides us. Only then can we see, smell, speak to, hear, think about, touch and know something other than ourselves.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-32.plain: Yajnavalkya tells King Janaka that the one true Seer is like an ocean, with nothing separate from it. This is the world of Brahman, the highest reality. It is a person's highest goal, success and joy, and all other beings live on just a small share of that joy.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-33.plain: Yajnavalkya compares joys. The best human life, healthy, rich and powerful, is one unit.
