Each higher world, of ancestors, heavenly musicians (Gandharvas), gods, and the creator Prajapati, holds a hundred times more joy than the one below, and Brahman's joy is highest. A learned person (Srotriya) who is free of wrongdoing and greed already has these joys. King Janaka offers a thousand gifts and asks for more teaching, and Yajnavalkya worries that the king, now so wise, will drive him from all his positions.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-34.plain: Yajnavalkya says that after a person has wandered through dreams, seeing good and bad things, he hurries back to where he began, the waking state.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-35.plain: When a person is about to die, the body moves along groaning, like an overloaded cart. It is carrying the conscious Self inside it.
themes: sitting with a dying loved one

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-36.plain: When the body becomes weak from old age or illness, the Self lets go of the limbs, the way a ripe mango or fig drops from its stem. Then it hurries on to a new life.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-37.plain: Officials wait with food and drink for a king who is returning home. In the same way, all the elements of nature wait for the person who knows this truth, saying, "Here comes Brahman."

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-3-38.plain: Officials gather around a king who is leaving. In the same way, all the senses (pranas, the life powers) gather around the Self at the moment of death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-4-1.plain: Yajnavalkya goes on. When a dying person grows weak and seems to lose consciousness, the senses gather around the Self. Taking their light with it, the Self goes down into the heart, and the eyes no longer see shapes.
themes: sitting with a dying loved one

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-4-2.plain: People around the dying person say he no longer sees, hears, speaks or knows, because all his senses have become one. The tip of the heart lights up, and by that light the Self leaves through the eye, the top of the head or another opening. The life breath and the other senses follow it. The Self stays aware, and it carries with it its knowledge, its past deeds and its old memories.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-4-3.plain: A caterpillar reaches the end of one blade of grass, grabs the next one and pulls itself over. In the same way, the Self drops this body and reaches toward another body.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-4-4.plain: A goldsmith melts a piece of gold into a newer, more beautiful shape. In the same way, the Self drops this body and makes itself a new and finer form. That form may be like the ancestors, the heavenly musicians (Gandharvas), the gods, the creator Prajapati, Brahman, or other beings.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-4-4-5.plain: The Self is Brahman, and it includes everything: mind, senses, the elements, desire and no desire, anger and no anger, right and wrong. We become what we do: good deeds make a person good and bad deeds make a person bad. A person is shaped by desire, because desire shapes the will, the will leads to actions, and we reap what our actions bring.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-4-2.plain: Ushasta complains that Yagnavalkya only described the Self the way you point at a cow or a horse, and asks again. Yagnavalkya says you cannot see the one who does the seeing, or hear the one who does the hearing, or know the one who does the knowing; that inner witness is your Self, and everything apart from it brings suffering.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-5-1.plain: Kahola asks about the Self within all, and Yagnavalkya says it is the one beyond hunger, thirst, sorrow, passion, old age and death. Wise people who know it stop chasing children, money and future worlds, because all of these are just desires. They go from learning, to real inner strength, to becoming a Muni (a silent sage), and finally become true knowers of Brahman, the ultimate reality. Everything else, he says, is bad.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-6-1.plain: Gargi, a woman scholar, asks Yagnavalkya what everything is woven into, like threads on a loom, and he answers step by step: water in air, air in the sky, and so on up to the worlds of Brahman, the ultimate reality. When she asks what Brahman is woven into, he warns her to stop, because that final reality cannot be reached by more questions.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-1.plain: Uddalaka tells how a spirit once asked his teacher about the hidden thread that ties this world, the next world and all beings together, and about the inner ruler who guides them from inside. He challenges Yagnavalkya to explain these, or else lose his head for taking the prize cows. Yagnavalkya says he knows, and Uddalaka says anyone can claim that, so prove it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-2.plain: Yagnavalkya says the thread is air, or the life-breath, which holds this world, the next world and all creatures together. That is why people say a dead person's limbs have come undone. Uddalaka agrees and asks him to explain the inner ruler next.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-3.plain: Yagnavalkya says the inner ruler lives inside the earth and guides it from within, using the earth as its body, yet the earth does not know it. This inner ruler is your own deathless Self.
themes: the hidden presence in the world

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-4.plain: The same inner ruler lives within water and guides it from inside, though water does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-5.plain: The inner ruler also lives within fire and guides it from inside, though fire does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-6.plain: The inner ruler lives within the sky and guides it from inside, though the sky does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-7.plain: The inner ruler lives within the air and guides it from inside, though the air does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-8.plain: The inner ruler lives within the heavens and guides them from inside, though the heavens do not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-9.plain: The inner ruler lives within the sun and guides it from inside, though the sun does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-10.plain: The inner ruler lives within the directions of space and guides them from inside, though they do not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-11.plain: The inner ruler lives within the moon and stars and guides them from inside, though they do not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-12.plain: The inner ruler lives within open space (akasha, the empty space everything sits in) and guides it from inside, though space does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-13.plain: The inner ruler lives even within darkness and guides it from inside, though darkness does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-14.plain: The inner ruler lives within light and guides it from inside, though light does not know it; it is your own deathless Self. This ends the list of forces of nature, and Yagnavalkya now turns to living beings.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-15.plain: Yagnavalkya says the inner ruler lives inside all living beings and guides them from within, though they do not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-16.plain: The inner ruler lives within the breath and guides it from inside, though the breath does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-7-17.plain: The inner ruler lives within speech and guides it from inside, though speech does not know it. It is your own deathless Self.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-13.plain: God is the one lasting thing behind everything that lasts, and the mind behind every mind. Though he is one, he answers the wishes of many. Whoever comes to know him, through careful thinking (Sankhya) and spiritual practice (Yoga), is set free from everything that binds them.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-14.plain: In God's world, the sun, moon, stars, lightning and fire give no light of their own. God is the true light. Everything else shines only because he shines.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-15.plain: God is like a single bird in the middle of the world, and like the sun's fire that has set into the ocean. Whoever truly knows him goes beyond death. There is no other way.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-16.plain: God made everything and knows everything. Nothing caused him. He is even the master of time. He rules nature and people and the three basic forces of nature (the gunas). He is the reason we are held in this world, the reason the world exists, and the reason we can be set free.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-17.plain: God is immortal and always present. He knows all and guards this world. He rules it forever, because no one else could.
themes: who is in charge of the world

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-18.plain: The speaker says: wanting to be free, I turn to God for safety. God is lit by his own thoughts. He first made Brahma, the creator god, and gave him the Vedas, the holy scriptures.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-19.plain: This God has no parts and does no actions. He is calm, with no fault and no stain. He is the best bridge to a life beyond death. He is like a fire that has burned up all its wood.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-20.plain: People could roll up the sky like a sheet of leather sooner than they could end their suffering without knowing God. Knowing God is the only real end to misery.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-21.plain: The wise sage Shvetashvatara, through his hard spiritual discipline and by God's grace, taught this highest and holiest truth about Brahman, the ultimate reality. He taught it to the most dedicated seekers, and the gathered sages approved it.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-22.plain: This deepest secret of the Upanishads, taught long ago, should not be given to someone who has not controlled their desires. It is only for one's own son or a true student.

upanishads-shvetashvatara-6-23.plain: When these truths are taught to a person with a noble heart, who loves God deeply and loves their teacher (guru) as much as God, the truths will truly shine and become clear to them.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-1-7.plain: Asvala, a priest at King Janaka's court, keeps testing the sage Yagnavalkya. He asks how many verses from the Rig Veda the Hotri priest (the one who recites) will use. Yagnavalkya names three kinds and says that through them the priest wins everything that breathes.
themes: a sage is tested in debate

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-1-8.plain: Asvala asks about the three kinds of offerings the Adhvaryu priest pours into the fire. Yagnavalkya says offerings that blaze up win the world of the gods. Those that crackle loudly win the world of the ancestors. Those that sink down win the world of humans.
themes: a sage is tested in debate

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-1-9.plain: Asvala asks how many gods the Brahman priest, who sits on the right and watches over the ritual, uses to protect it. Yagnavalkya says only one: the mind. The mind is endless, like the countless gods called the Visvedevas, so through it the priest wins an endless world.
themes: a sage is tested in debate

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-1-10.plain: Asvala asks about the three hymns the Udgatri priest (the one who chants) will sing. Yagnavalkya links the three hymns to three kinds of breath in the body. He says they win the earth, the sky and heaven. After this Asvala falls silent, defeated.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-1.plain: A new challenger, Artabhaga, asks Yagnavalkya about the eight 'graspers' and the eight 'over-graspers'. These are things that seize us and the things that seize them in turn. Yagnavalkya says there are eight of each.
themes: a sage is tested in debate

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-2.plain: Yagnavalkya says the breath is a grasper. It is held in turn by the down-breath, because we smell with the down-breath.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-3.plain: Speech is a grasper, and it is held by names, because we use speech to say names.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-4.plain: The tongue is a grasper, and it is held by taste, because we taste with the tongue.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-5.plain: The eye is a grasper, and it is held by the things it sees, because we see shapes and colors with the eye.
themes: drawn in by what we see

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-6.plain: The ear is a grasper, and it is held by sound, because we hear sounds with the ear.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-7.plain: The mind is a grasper, and it is held by desire, because we want things with the mind.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-8.plain: The arms are a grasper, and they are held by work, because we do our work with our arms.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-9.plain: The skin is a grasper, and it is held by touch, because we feel touch through the skin. Yagnavalkya says these are all eight graspers and their eight over-graspers.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-10.plain: Artabhaga says everything is eaten by death, and asks what eats death itself. Yagnavalkya answers that fire is death, yet water puts out fire. So even death can be overcome.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-11.plain: Artabhaga asks whether the life-breaths leave a wise person when they die. Yagnavalkya says no. The breaths gather inside the body, it swells, and the dead body lies at rest.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-12.plain: Artabhaga asks what stays with a person after death. Yagnavalkya says the name, because a name lasts without end. Through it the person wins an endless world.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-2-13.plain: Artabhaga asks where a person really is once every part has gone back to nature: speech to fire, breath to wind, eyes to the sun, body to the earth. Yagnavalkya takes his hand and says they should discuss this privately. Alone, they agree the answer is karma (one's actions): a person becomes good by good deeds and bad by bad deeds.
themes: where do we go after death

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-3-1.plain: Another challenger, Bhujyu, tells a story from his student days. A girl was possessed by a Gandharva, a heavenly spirit. The students asked the spirit where the Parikshitas, a line of old kings, went after death. Now Bhujyu asks Yagnavalkya the same question.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-3-2.plain: Yagnavalkya says the Parikshitas went where those who did the great horse sacrifice go. He describes the world, the earth and the ocean around it, with a gap as thin as a razor's edge. The god Indra, as a bird, passed them through the gap to Vayu, the wind, who carried them there. So the wind is everything, and whoever knows this overcomes death.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-3-4-1.plain: Ushasta asks Yagnavalkya to show him the Self (atman), the true inner being that lives in everyone. Yagnavalkya says it is your own Self. It is the one who breathes in, breathes out and breathes through you.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-20.plain: Breath is also called Brihaspati, a name meaning "lord of speech." Speech is called Brihati, a name for the Rig Veda's verses, and breath is its master, since we need breath to speak.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-21.plain: Breath is also called Brahmanaspati, because speech is the holy word and breath rules it. Breath is also the Saman, the sung chant of the Sama Veda. The word joins "sa" (speech) and "ama" (breath), because singing needs both.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-22.plain: Breath is called Saman for another reason too. "Sama" means "equal," and the same breath lives in a tiny bug, a gnat, an elephant and the whole universe. Whoever understands this becomes one with it.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-23.plain: Breath is also the Udgitha, the main chant sung at a sacrifice. "Ut" stands for breath, which holds up the whole world, and "githa" means song, which is speech. Together they make the word Udgitha.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-24.plain: Brahmadatta, grandson of Kikitana, swore an oath while drinking Soma, the sacred ritual drink. He said the sage Ayasya Angirasa sang the chant using nothing but speech and breath, and he would lose his head if this were not true.
themes: the story of the sage's chant

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-25.plain: The true wealth of the chant is a good tone of voice. So a priest who sings at a sacrifice should want a fine, clear voice. People choose a priest with a good voice the way they would choose a rich man. Whoever knows this gains wealth.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-26.plain: The gold of the chant is also its good tone. Whoever knows this gains gold.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-27.plain: The chant rests on speech, because breath is sung through speech. When the singing starts, the worshipper should pray: "Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality." Both "unreal" and "darkness" mean death, so all three lines ask the same thing: "Make me immortal."
themes: longing for light in dark times

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-3-28.plain: During the other chants, the worshipper may ask for any wish he has. A priest who understands this chant can win, by his singing, whatever is wished for himself or for the worshipper. This knowledge is called the conqueror of worlds. Whoever has it need not fear being shut out of any world.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-1.plain: At first only the Self existed, in the shape of a person. He looked around and saw nothing else, so his first words were "This is I." That is why people still say "It's me" before giving their name. The text explains the word purusha (person) as the one who burned away all evil before anything else existed.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-2.plain: Being alone, he felt afraid, and that is why lonely people feel fear. Then he thought, "There is nothing here but me, so what is there to fear?" and his fear went away. Fear only comes when there is someone or something other than yourself.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-3.plain: He still felt no joy, which is why a lonely person feels no joy. He wanted a companion, so he split himself in two, and husband and wife came into being. The sage Yajnavalkya said a married couple are like the two halves of one shell, and a wife or husband fills the empty half. From their union, people were born.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-4.plain: The wife thought it was wrong for him to unite with her, since she came from him, so she hid by turning into a cow. He became a bull, and cows were born. They kept changing into horses, donkeys, goats and sheep, and so every kind of creature that comes in pairs was made, down to the ants.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-5.plain: He realized, "I am this whole creation, because I made all of it." So he became the creation. Whoever knows this feels at home in that creation.
themes: feeling at home in the world

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-6.plain: Next he made fire from his mouth and hands. All the gods people worship are really just forms of him, because he is every god. The world is made of food and eaters: Soma, the moist offering, is food, and Agni, the fire, is the eater. His highest creation was making the undying gods even though he himself was then mortal.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-7.plain: At first the world had no shape. Then it took on names and forms. The Self entered everything, right to the fingertips, hidden like a razor in its case. When it breathes we call it breath, when it sees we call it eye, but these are only names for what it does. Worship it as the whole Self, because it is like a footprint that leads you to everything.
themes: seeing the whole, not the parts

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-8.plain: The Self is closer to us than anything. It is dearer than a child, dearer than money, dearer than everything else. If you love something other than the Self most, you may well lose it. If you love the Self most, what you love will never die.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-9.plain: People ask a question: if knowing Brahman, the ultimate reality, lets us become everything, then what did Brahman itself know, from which the whole world came?

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-10.plain: In the beginning Brahman knew only itself, saying "I am Brahman," and everything came from that. Any god, sage or person who wakes up to this becomes Brahman too. The sage Vamadeva realized it and sang, "I was Manu, I was the sun." A person who worships a god as separate from himself does not truly understand. The gods even prefer that people do not learn this, because people serve them like farm animals serve a man.
themes: freedom from fear of the gods

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-11.plain: At first Brahman was alone and not strong enough. So it created rulers and powerful gods like Indra, Varuna and Yama. That is why kings rank so high, and why the priest sits below the king at the royal crowning ceremony. Yet priestly wisdom is where royal power comes from, so a king who harms a priest harms his own source and becomes worse.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-12.plain: The story of creation goes on. Brahman, the one source of everything, still did not feel complete. So it made the common people among the gods. These are groups of gods called the Vasus, Rudras, Adityas, Visve Devas and Maruts.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-13.plain: Brahman still did not feel complete. So it made the Sudra class, the workers, in the form of Pushan, the god who feeds and nourishes. The earth itself is Pushan, because the earth feeds every living thing.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-14.plain: Brahman still did not feel complete, so it created dharma, which means law or what is right. Right is stronger than any ruler, so nothing stands above it. Because of it, even a weak person can stand up to a strong one, as if a king were backing them. Right and truth are the same thing: speaking the truth is speaking what is right.
themes: when the weak face the powerful

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-15.plain: Brahman showed up among the gods as fire and among people as the four social classes. But a person who dies without knowing their true inner Self loses what they gained. Even great good deeds will not last for them in the end. A person who worships the Self as their true home keeps the fruit of their work and gets what they wish for.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-16.plain: Every person supports many beings. By offering to the gods, a person feeds the gods. By reciting sacred hymns, they honor the ancient sages. By honoring the ancestors and raising children, they serve the ancestors. By feeding guests and caring for animals, they serve people and animals. Even the birds and ants living in their home depend on them. So all beings want such a person to be safe and well.
themes: our duties to family and ancestors

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-4-17.plain: In the beginning the Self was alone and wished for a wife, children, and wealth for religious offerings. That is why lonely people feel incomplete until they have these things. But a person is already complete inside. The mind is like the husband and speech is like the wife. The breath is like the child. The eye brings worldly wealth and the ear brings spiritual wealth. The body is how they do their work.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-1.plain: This is an old verse with riddles. The father of creation made seven kinds of food. One kind is shared by all beings, two are for the gods, three are for himself, and one is for the animals. Everything depends on this food. The verse asks why food never runs out even though it is always being eaten. Whoever knows the answer lives with strength and reaches the gods.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-2.plain: The text explains the riddle. The shared food is the everyday food everyone eats. A person who only lives for that food is not free from wrongdoing, because it belongs to everyone. The two foods for the gods are the offerings into fire and the gifts given at a ritual. The food for animals is milk, which every newborn lives on. Food never runs out because the Person, the inner Self, keeps making it again and again.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-3.plain: The three foods the creator kept for himself are mind, speech, and breath. We really see and hear with the mind. That is why people say, 'My mind was elsewhere, I didn't hear.' Desire, doubt, faith, memory, shame, and fear all belong to the mind. All sound is speech. All kinds of breathing are breath. A person is made of these three.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-4.plain: Speech, mind, and breath are matched with the three worlds. Speech is the earth, mind is the sky, and breath is heaven.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-5.plain: Speech, mind, and breath are also matched with the three Vedas, the ancient holy books. Speech is the Rig Veda, mind is the Yajur Veda, and breath is the Sama Veda.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-6.plain: Speech, mind, and breath are also the three kinds of beings. Speech is the gods, mind is the ancestors, and breath is living people.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-7.plain: Speech, mind, and breath are also like a family. The mind is the father, speech is the mother, and breath is the child.
themes: family as a picture of life

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-8.plain: What we already know takes the form of speech, because speech is clear and known. Speech, in this role, protects a person.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-9.plain: What we are still trying to know takes the form of mind, because the mind is always working things out. The mind, in this role, protects a person.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-10.plain: What is unknown takes the form of breath, because breath is hidden and hard to grasp. Breath, in this role, protects a person.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-11.plain: Speech has the earth as its body and fire as its light. Speech reaches as far as the earth and fire reach.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-12.plain: The mind has heaven as its body and the sun as its light. It reaches as far as heaven and the sun. When fire and sun come together, wind is born, and the wind is Indra, king of the gods, who has no rival. Rivals only exist when there is a second, so whoever understands this has no rival.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-13.plain: Breath has water as its body and the moon as its light. Speech, mind, and breath are equal and endless. If you think of them as small and limited, you get a small life. If you see them as endless, you get an endless world.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-14.plain: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, is the year, and he has sixteen parts like the phases of the moon. Fifteen parts are the nights that grow and shrink, and one part stays fixed. On the new-moon night he enters every living thing and is born again in the morning. So on that night no one should kill any living creature, not even a lizard.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-15.plain: A person who understands this is like Prajapati (the creator god), who is pictured as the year. His wealth is like the outer rim of a wheel and his true Self is the hub at the center. Wealth comes and goes, but if he loses everything and still has his Self, people say he only lost the rim, which can be replaced.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-16.plain: There are three worlds: the world of people, the world of the ancestors (the Fathers), and the world of the gods (Devas). You keep a place in the human world through a son, reach the ancestors' world through sacrifice, and reach the gods' world through knowledge. The gods' world is best, so knowledge is praised most.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-17.plain: When a father feels he is about to die, he hands his duties to his son, saying, 'You are the Veda (the sacred learning), you are the sacrifice, you are the world.' The son accepts them. The father feels his son will carry on his work and make up for his mistakes, and so the father's speech, mind, and breath live on in the son.
themes: passing on to the next generation

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-18.plain: Holy speech comes into such a person from the earth and from fire. Holy speech is speech where whatever he says comes true.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-19.plain: Holy mind comes into him from the sky and the sun. Holy mind is the kind of mind that makes a person happy and free from grief.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-20.plain: Holy breath comes into him from water and the moon. This breath never gets tired and never dies. Whoever knows this becomes one with all beings, like the great god Hiranyagarbha, and is honored by all. Grief leaves him, and only good comes near him.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-21.plain: Prajapati created the senses, and they argued over who was best: speech wanted to speak, the eye to see, the ear to hear. Death came as tiredness and wore them out, but it could not touch the central breath. So the senses all took breath's form, which is why they are called 'breaths.' A family with someone who knows this is named after him.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-22.plain: The same happened among the gods. Fire wanted to burn, the sun to warm, the moon to shine. Like breath among the senses, Vayu, the wind, was the one that never fades. The others set or go out, but the wind never stops.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-5-23.plain: A verse says the sun rises and sets in breath, and the gods made breath the lasting law. So a person should keep one practice: breathing in and breathing out, so death does not reach him. If he keeps it up to the end, he becomes one with breath, the life-force (prana).

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-6-1.plain: The world is made of three things: name, form, and action. For all names, speech is their source, it is the same as them, and it holds them up.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-6-2.plain: For all forms and shapes, the eye is their source, it is the same as them, and it holds them up.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-1-6-3.plain: For all actions, the body is their source, the same as them, and their support. These three, name, form, and action, are really one thing: the Self. The undying breath is hidden inside the passing world of names and forms.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-1.plain: Gargya Balaki, a proud and well-read man, offered to teach King Ajatashatru of Kashi about Brahman, the ultimate reality. The king happily offered a thousand cows, saying people usually run to King Janaka for such teaching.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-2.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in the sun as Brahman. The king stopped him: he already honors that one as the supreme ruler of all beings, and whoever does so becomes a supreme ruler too.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-3.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in the moon as Brahman. The king said he already honors that one as great, dressed in white, as Soma the king, and whoever does so never runs out of food.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-4.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in lightning as Brahman. The king said he already honors that one as shining, and whoever does so becomes bright, and so do his children.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-5.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in space as Brahman. The king said he already honors that one as full and still, and whoever does so is blessed with children and cattle, and his family line lasts.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-6.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in the wind as Brahman. The king said he already honors that one as Indra, the unbeatable army of storm gods, and whoever does so wins and cannot be defeated.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-7.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in fire as Brahman. The king said he already honors that one as powerful, and whoever does so becomes strong, and so do his children.

upanishads-brihadaranyaka-2-1-8.plain: Gargya said he worships the person in water as Brahman. The king said he already honors that one as likeness, and whoever does so receives what is right and fitting, and his children are like him.
